tracks.title: Design Thinking
tracks.blurb: A human-centred way to frame problems and test ideas quickly. Start here.

lessons.s: Understand people before you design for them.
lessons.c: Empathy is the work of understanding what people do, think and feel in their own context. You set aside your assumptions and gather evidence through interviews, observation and immersion.
lessons.e: A team redesigning a campus dining app spends a lunch hour watching students order. Most people order one-handed while carrying a tray, which no survey had revealed.
lessons.y: Interview one classmate for 10 minutes about how they plan their week. Ask "Tell me about the last time…" instead of "Would you…". Write down three quotes word for word.
lessons.k: Observe behaviour, not opinions. What people do tells you more than what they say.

lessons.s: Turn research into a clear problem statement.
lessons.c: In the Define stage you synthesise findings into a point-of-view statement: a specific user, their need, and the insight behind it. A sharp problem statement keeps the team from solving the wrong thing.
lessons.e: "Commuter students need a way to find a quiet study spot between classes because the library fills up by 10am." It names who, what and why.
lessons.y: Write a "How might we…" question from your interview notes. Make it narrow enough to act on and broad enough to allow many answers.
lessons.k: A good problem statement is about people, not features.

lessons.s: Generate many ideas before judging any.
lessons.c: Ideation means producing lots of possible solutions first, then clustering and choosing. Useful methods include brainstorming, Crazy 8s, mind maps and SCAMPER.
lessons.e: In Crazy 8s you fold a sheet into eight panels and sketch eight ideas in eight minutes. The time limit stops you from polishing the first idea.
lessons.y: Run a solo Crazy 8s on your "How might we" question. Circle the idea you would test first and the one that scares you most.
lessons.k: Defer judgement. The best idea is rarely the first one.

lessons.s: Make ideas real enough to test.
lessons.c: A prototype is a cheap, testable version of an idea. Low fidelity (paper, wireframes) answers "does this make sense?". High fidelity (interactive Figma) answers "does this feel right?".
lessons.e: A paper prototype of a checkout flow can be tested in an afternoon. Changing a step costs a pencil line instead of a sprint.
lessons.y: Sketch the three key screens of your idea on paper or in FigJam. Link them so someone can tap through the main task.
lessons.k: Build only what you need to learn the next thing.

lessons.s: Watch real people use your prototype.
lessons.c: Testing puts your prototype in front of real users to see where they succeed and struggle. You give a task, stay quiet and watch. Five users usually reveal most of the major usability problems.
lessons.e: A student tester tries to "book a study room" and taps the calendar icon three times before finding the button. That hesitation is your data.
lessons.y: Give your prototype to two people. Ask them to think aloud while completing one task. Note every pause, wrong tap and question.
lessons.k: Testing feeds back into empathy, and the loop starts again.

tracks.title: Gestalt Principles
tracks.sub: How eyes group what they see
tracks.blurb: Six principles of visual perception that explain why layouts feel organised or messy.

lessons.s: Things close together look related.
lessons.c: Elements placed close together are seen as a group. Spacing alone can show structure without lines or boxes.
lessons.e: On a sign-up form, each label sits closer to its own field than to the field above. Users instantly know which label belongs where.
lessons.y: Open any app's settings screen. Find where spacing, not dividers, separates the groups.
lessons.k: Space is a design element. Use it to show relationships.

lessons.s: Things that look alike feel alike.
lessons.c: Elements that share colour, shape or size are perceived as related, even when they are spread apart.
lessons.e: Every tappable link in an article is the same blue. Users learn the pattern once and spot links everywhere.
lessons.y: Find a UI where two different actions look the same. How could you make the difference visible?
lessons.k: Make things that work the same look the same.

lessons.s: We complete shapes that are not there.
lessons.c: Our brains fill in missing parts to see a complete shape. Designers use this for logos and icons that feel simple yet whole.
lessons.e: The IBM logo is built from horizontal stripes with gaps, yet we read solid letters.
lessons.y: Sketch an icon for "library" with as few strokes as possible. Remove lines until it stops being recognisable.
lessons.k: Suggest the shape and let the viewer complete it.

lessons.s: The eye follows lines and curves.
lessons.c: The eye follows lines and curves, and prefers continuous paths over abrupt changes in direction.
lessons.e: A card row that cuts the last card in half invites you to swipe for more. The Design Thinking row on this app's Home screen does exactly that.
lessons.y: Look at three apps you use daily. Find one element that hints there is more content off-screen.
lessons.k: Align elements along a path to guide the eye.

lessons.s: We split scenes into object and background.
lessons.c: We separate what we see into a foreground object (figure) and a background (ground). Modals, cards and dimmed overlays rely on this.
lessons.e: When a bottom sheet opens, the screen behind dims. The sheet becomes the figure and takes your focus.
lessons.y: Open any term in the Glossary tab and notice how the dimmed background changes where you look.
lessons.k: Contrast tells users what to look at first.

lessons.s: A boundary makes a group.
lessons.c: Items inside the same bounded area are seen as a group, even when they are not close together or similar.
lessons.e: Shopping sites put image, title and price inside one card, so they read as one product.
lessons.y: Find a screen where a container groups items that look unrelated. Does it work?
lessons.k: A boundary is a strong grouping cue. Use it sparingly.

tracks.title: Laws of UX
tracks.blurb: Research-backed rules of thumb that explain how people perceive, decide and act.

lessons.s: Big, close targets are faster to hit.
lessons.c: The time to reach a target depends on its distance and size. Larger, closer targets are faster and easier to hit.
lessons.e: On mobile, primary buttons sit within thumb reach at the bottom of the screen and often span the full width.
lessons.y: Find the smallest button in an app you use. Apple recommends touch targets of at least 44×44 points.
lessons.k: Make important targets big and easy to reach.

lessons.s: More choices, slower decisions.
lessons.c: The time it takes to decide grows with the number and complexity of choices.
lessons.e: Streaming apps show a short row of top picks before the full catalogue, so you can decide quickly.
lessons.y: Count the options on a food delivery home screen. Which could be hidden until needed?
lessons.k: Reduce choices, or break them into steps.

lessons.s: Users expect your app to work like others.
lessons.c: People spend most of their time on other products, so they expect yours to work the same way.
lessons.e: The cart icon lives in the top-right corner. Moving it to be creative costs users time.
lessons.y: List three conventions every shopping app follows. Would breaking any of them help users?
lessons.k: Innovate where it matters. Follow conventions everywhere else.

lessons.s: Chunk information to help memory.
lessons.c: Working memory holds a limited number of items, roughly seven give or take two. Chunking content into groups makes it easier to process.
lessons.e: Phone numbers are split into chunks: 555 012 3456 is easier to remember than 5550123456.
lessons.y: Rewrite a long paragraph from your notes as three short chunks with headings.
lessons.k: Chunk information. Don't treat "seven" as a hard limit for menus.

lessons.s: Beautiful feels easier to use.
lessons.c: People perceive attractive designs as easier to use and are more forgiving of small problems in them.
lessons.e: In usability tests, polished prototypes can hide real issues because testers forgive them.
lessons.y: Test the same flow as a wireframe and as a styled mockup. Compare the feedback you get.
lessons.k: Beauty builds trust, but it can mask problems during testing.

lessons.s: Respond in under 400 ms.
lessons.c: Productivity rises when a system responds in under about 400 milliseconds, so neither the person nor the computer is waiting.
lessons.e: Skeleton screens and instant button feedback make apps feel fast while data is still loading.
lessons.y: Tap through this app. Every tap responds immediately. Notice how that feels.
lessons.k: Give feedback fast, even when the result takes longer.

tracks.title: AI for Designers
tracks.sub: Use AI as a creative partner
tracks.blurb: How to use AI in research, ideation and prototyping, and how to design AI products responsibly.

lessons.s: A collaborator, not a replacement.
lessons.c: AI tools can speed up research synthesis, ideation, copywriting, image generation and prototyping. They work best as a collaborator: you set direction and judge quality, the tool produces options.
lessons.e: A designer pastes 20 anonymised interview notes into an AI assistant, asks for recurring themes, then checks every theme against the original quotes.
lessons.y: List the steps of your last design project. Mark where AI could save time and where human judgement is essential.
lessons.k: AI speeds up the work. Your judgement decides what is good.

lessons.s: Role, context, task, constraints, format.
lessons.c: A strong prompt gives a role, context, a clear task, constraints and the format you want back. Vague prompts get generic output.
lessons.e: Weak: "Give me app ideas." Strong: "You are a UX researcher. Based on these five pain points from first-year students, suggest 10 How might we questions, each under 15 words."
lessons.y: Rewrite one vague prompt using role, context, task, constraints and format. Compare both outputs side by side.
lessons.k: Be specific, and iterate on prompts the way you iterate on designs.

lessons.s: Fast clustering, careful checking.
lessons.c: AI can transcribe interviews, cluster notes into affinity groups and draft personas. It can also invent details, so verify everything against your raw data.
lessons.e: An AI-generated persona says students "prefer dark mode". No participant said that. The model made it up.
lessons.y: Ask an AI tool to summarise a set of notes. Highlight every claim you cannot trace back to a source.
lessons.k: Only use findings you can trace to real evidence, and protect participants' privacy.

lessons.s: Generate wide, refine deep.
lessons.c: Tools such as Figma's AI features, Uizard and Claude can turn prompts or sketches into layouts and working prototypes. Use them to explore directions quickly, then refine by hand.
lessons.e: A team generates five layout options for a dashboard in minutes, picks one, and rebuilds it properly in their design system.
lessons.y: Describe your idea's main screen in one paragraph and ask an AI tool to build it. Critique the result using the Gestalt principles.
lessons.k: Generate wide, then refine deep.

lessons.s: Set expectations, keep users in control.
lessons.c: Users of AI features need to know what the system can do, how confident it is, and how to correct it. Google's People + AI Guidebook and Microsoft's HAX Toolkit collect proven patterns.
lessons.e: A writing assistant shows suggestions in grey. You accept with Tab or ignore by typing, so you always stay in control.
lessons.y: Pick an AI feature you use. How does it show errors or uncertainty? Sketch one improvement.
lessons.k: Explain outputs, show confidence and always let users override.

lessons.s: You are accountable for what you ship.
lessons.c: AI models learn from data that can carry bias. Designers need to check outputs for stereotypes, respect creators' rights and be open about where AI was used.
lessons.e: An image generator asked for "a designer" returns mostly one gender and ethnicity. A responsible designer adjusts the prompt and reviews results.
lessons.y: Generate eight images of "a student studying". Note who is represented and who is missing.
lessons.k: You are accountable for your work, whoever or whatever generated it.

tracks.title: Immersive & Emerging Tech
tracks.sub: VR, AR, spatial and game UX
tracks.blurb: Design beyond the flat screen: extended reality, 3D prototyping, games and voice.

lessons.s: The extended reality spectrum.
lessons.c: Virtual reality replaces your surroundings. Augmented reality overlays digital content on the real world. Mixed reality lets digital objects interact with physical space. Together they are called extended reality, or XR.
lessons.e: IKEA Place uses AR to put true-to-scale furniture in your room before you buy it.
lessons.y: Try one AR experience on your phone, such as a measuring or furniture app. Note what felt natural and what felt awkward.
lessons.k: Choose the medium that fits the task, not the hype.

lessons.s: Design for bodies, not just screens.
lessons.c: In XR the interface lives in 3D space. Place content at a comfortable distance, avoid making people look sharply up or down, and keep text large with strong contrast.
lessons.e: Apple's visionOS guidelines place windows in front of the user at a comfortable distance and use eye gaze plus a pinch to select.
lessons.y: Sketch a floating menu for a VR museum tour. Where does it appear relative to the visitor's head and hands?
lessons.k: Comfort comes first in spatial design.

lessons.s: No code needed to start.
lessons.c: You can prototype XR without code. ShapesXR, Bezi and Spline let you build and test spatial scenes. Unity and Unreal take them further.
lessons.e: A student team builds a VR campus orientation tour in ShapesXR and tests it in a headset before writing any code.
lessons.y: Open Spline in your browser and build a simple 3D card that tilts when you hover over it.
lessons.k: Prototype in the medium. Flat mockups miss depth and scale.

lessons.s: Teach through play.
lessons.c: Game UX shapes how players learn, feel and stay engaged: onboarding, feedback, HUD clarity and difficulty curves. Celia Hodent's work applies cognitive science to player experience.
lessons.e: Many platformers teach in the first level by introducing one mechanic at a time, with no text tutorial.
lessons.y: Play the first five minutes of a game. List each thing it teaches you and how it does it.
lessons.k: Teach by doing. Feedback is how a game talks to the player.

lessons.s: Pick the right input for the moment.
lessons.c: Interfaces increasingly combine voice, touch, gaze and gesture. Voice is fast for commands, touch is precise, and gaze is quick for pointing.
lessons.e: A driver says "navigate home" instead of tapping through menus, keeping their eyes on the road.
lessons.y: Script a short voice conversation for booking a study room. Plan what happens when the assistant mishears.
lessons.k: Match the input to the context, and design for errors.

terms.d: Showing two versions of a design to different groups of users to see which performs better against a goal.
terms.ex: Testing two button labels, "Join" and "Get started", to see which gets more sign-ups.

terms.d: Designing so people with disabilities can perceive, understand and use a product. Often shortened to a11y.
terms.ex: Adding text alternatives to images so screen reader users hear what the image shows.

terms.d: A way to organise research notes by grouping related observations to reveal themes.
terms.ex: Clustering 60 sticky notes from interviews into groups like "time pressure" and "cost".

terms.d: A property of an object that suggests how it can be used.
terms.ex: A raised button looks pressable. A slider handle looks draggable.

terms.d: Technology that overlays digital content on a live view of the real world.
terms.ex: Seeing a virtual sofa placed in your living room through your phone camera.

terms.d: The element that prompts the user to take the main next step.
terms.ex: "Start lesson" is the call to action on a course page.

terms.d: A method where participants group topics into categories to help shape information architecture.
terms.ex: Students sort 30 course topics into groups that make sense to them.

terms.d: The mental effort needed to use an interface. Lower load means easier use.
terms.ex: A form that asks for one thing per screen reduces cognitive load.

terms.d: The difference in brightness between text and its background. WCAG asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text.
terms.ex: Light grey text on white often fails the 4.5:1 minimum.

terms.d: A design that tricks users into doing something they did not intend.
terms.ex: A pre-ticked box that signs you up for marketing emails.

terms.d: A shared set of reusable components, styles and guidelines that keeps a product consistent.
terms.ex: Google's Material Design is a public design system.

terms.d: A canvas that captures what a user says, thinks, does and feels.
terms.ex: Filling in an empathy map right after a user interview.

terms.d: How closely a prototype resembles the final product, from low (sketches) to high (interactive and polished).
terms.ex: Paper sketches are low fidelity. A clickable Figma prototype is high fidelity.

terms.d: The extent of the scene visible at one time in a headset, measured in degrees.
terms.ex: Placing key UI in the centre of the field of view so users don't turn their heads.

terms.d: AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio or code from a prompt.
terms.ex: Generating mood board images from a text description.

terms.d: When an AI model produces confident but false or made-up information.
terms.ex: An AI summary quoting a participant who never said that.

terms.d: An expert review of an interface against established usability principles, such as Nielsen's 10 heuristics.
terms.ex: Checking whether every error message explains how to recover.

terms.d: A question format that reframes a problem as an opportunity for ideas.
terms.ex: "How might we help commuter students find quiet study spots?"

terms.d: A setup where people review, correct or approve AI output before it takes effect.
terms.ex: A designer approves AI-generated alt text before publishing.

terms.d: How content is organised, labelled and connected so people can find what they need.
terms.ex: The map of screens in this app: Home, Learn, Glossary, Resources, Progress.

terms.d: Repeating a cycle of design, test and refine to improve a product step by step.
terms.ex: Version 3 of a prototype fixes issues found while testing version 2.

terms.d: A visual of the steps a person goes through to reach a goal, including their feelings at each step.
terms.ex: Mapping a freshman's first week, from orientation to the first assignment.

terms.d: An AI model trained on large amounts of text to understand and generate language.
terms.ex: Claude and other chat assistants are built on LLMs.

terms.d: A person's internal understanding of how something works, which shapes their expectations.
terms.ex: People expect a trash icon to delete things.

terms.d: A small, focused moment of feedback for a single action.
terms.ex: A heart icon that pops when you like a post.

terms.d: The simplest version of a product that delivers value and lets you learn from real users.
terms.ex: Launching with only the glossary before adding lessons.

terms.d: Experiences where digital objects are anchored to, and interact with, the physical world.
terms.ex: A virtual ball that bounces off your real table.

terms.d: A static, visually detailed picture of a design that shows how it will look.
terms.ex: A polished Figma frame of the home screen without interactions.

terms.d: The first experience that helps new users understand and start using a product.
terms.ex: A three-step intro that asks students which track to start with.

terms.d: A specific problem or frustration a user experiences.
terms.ex: "I can never find which room my seminar is in."

terms.d: A fictional profile based on research that represents a key group of users.
terms.ex: "Maya, 18, first-gen student, studies on the bus."

terms.d: The feeling of actually being inside a virtual environment.
terms.ex: Flinching when a virtual object flies toward you.

terms.d: The instruction or input you give an AI model.
terms.ex: "Suggest 10 names for a study app, each under 12 letters."

terms.d: An early, testable model of a design used to learn before building.
terms.ex: A clickable flow for booking a study room.

terms.d: Layouts that adapt to different screen sizes and orientations.
terms.ex: A grid with three columns on desktop and one on a phone.

terms.d: Tracking that follows both head rotation and movement through space.
terms.ex: In a 6DoF headset you can lean in to look closer at an object.

terms.d: Computing that understands and blends with the 3D space around you.
terms.ex: Apps placed as windows around your room in a headset.

terms.d: Anyone with an interest in a project's outcome, such as clients, users or team members.
terms.ex: A course instructor reviewing your app concept.

terms.d: Watching real users try tasks with a product to find problems.
terms.ex: Asking a student to find the Gestalt lesson while you observe.

terms.d: The path a user takes through screens to complete a task.
terms.ex: Home → Lesson → Mark complete → Next lesson.

terms.d: A fully digital environment that replaces your view of the real world.
terms.ex: Touring a virtual campus in a headset.

terms.d: Arranging elements so their order of importance is clear through size, colour, contrast and position.
terms.ex: The page title is largest, then section headings, then body text.

terms.d: Empty space around and between elements that improves clarity and focus.
terms.ex: Generous margins around a key headline.

terms.d: A simple, low-fidelity layout that shows structure without visual styling.
terms.ex: Grey boxes showing where the image, title and button go.

hero.alt: A student interviews a classmate in a campus cafe, taking notes
hero.cap: A research interview: listen more than you talk.

p: You rarely get empathy from one conversation. Designers combine methods so they see both what people say and what they actually do.
defs: One-on-one conversations. Ask open questions about real past experiences, then follow up with "why?"
Watch people in their real context, such as a library, a dorm or a bus, without interrupting.
Do the task yourself. Try booking a study room on your phone while walking to class.

media.cap: Fill one quadrant at a time with notes from your research.

p: An empathy map sorts what you learned into four boxes: what the person says, thinks, does and feels. Gaps between "says" and "does" are often where the best insights hide.

w: empathy stage design thinking user interview tips

hero.alt: Students cluster sticky notes into groups on a studio wall
hero.cap: Synthesis: turning a wall of notes into a few clear themes.

deep.callout: [User] needs [a way to do something] because [insight from research].
p2: Example: "First-year commuter students need a reliable way to find a quiet study spot between classes, because the library is full by 10am and they waste their only free hour searching."

p: A "How might we" question opens the problem up for ideas without suggesting a solution.
defs: How might we add a room map to the app?
How might we help commuters find a quiet spot in under five minutes?

w: affinity diagram design thinking define stage

hero.alt: A sheet folded into eight panels with eight quick app sketches and a timer
hero.cap: A finished Crazy 8s sheet: eight ideas, eight minutes.

p: Whatever method you use, these rules keep ideas flowing:
defs: Aim for many ideas. Good ones often appear after the obvious ones are out of the way.
No "that won't work" yet. Critique comes later.
Say "yes, and…" to extend a teammate's idea.
An impossible idea can point to a practical one.
Keep your "How might we" question visible the whole time.

p: A short, focused group session, usually 15 to 20 minutes. Everyone writes one idea per sticky note, says it out loud, and puts it on the wall. One conversation at a time so ideas can build on each other.
Tip: brainstorm alone for five minutes first. Quieter teammates get their ideas down before louder voices set the direction.
A fast sketching exercise from the Google Ventures design sprint. It pushes you past your first idea.
steps: Fold a sheet of paper into eight panels.
Set a timer for eight minutes.
Sketch one idea per panel, about one minute each.
Keep it rough. Boxes, arrows and stick figures are fine.
Share your sheet and dot-vote on the strongest ideas.

media.cap: A mind map for "quiet study spots". Each branch is a theme you can explore.

p: Write the problem in the centre, then branch out into themes, and branch again into ideas. It helps you see connections and spot areas you have not explored yet.
SCAMPER is a checklist of seven questions that make you look at an existing product from new angles. Here it is applied to a study-room booking app:
defs: What could you replace? Swap the login form for a student ID scan.
What could you merge? Combine room booking with your class calendar.
What could you borrow? Adapt a restaurant waitlist for full study rooms.
What could be bigger or smaller? Show only the next free room, not a long list.
Where else could this work? Use booking data to show the quietest times.
What could you remove? Drop the confirmation email and show a QR pass.
What if you flipped it? Let free rooms notify nearby students.

media.cap: Plot each idea by how much it helps users and how hard it is to build.

p: After you generate, converge. Dot-vote as a team, then place the winners on an impact and effort grid. Quick wins are easy to test first. Big bets may be worth a bolder prototype.

hero.alt: A hand slides a paper app screen into a paper phone frame
hero.cap: Paper prototypes are fast to make and easy to change.

deep.h: Match the prototype to the question
defs: Paper or sketches. Is the flow understandable? Make it in minutes.
Grey-box wireframes in Figma. Is the layout and navigation right?
Styled, clickable screens. Does it feel right? Is the copy clear?

hero.alt: A student uses an app and thinks aloud while an observer takes notes

steps: Welcome the participant. Explain you are testing the design, not them.
Give a realistic task, like "Book a study room for 3pm today."
Ask them to think aloud while they work.
Stay quiet. Don't help, even when they struggle.
Ask follow-up questions at the end: "What did you expect to happen there?"
Note every pause, wrong tap and question. Fix the biggest issues and test again.

hero.alt: A design student works with an AI assistant on one screen and a design tool on the other
hero.cap: AI as a studio partner: you direct, it drafts.

defs: Transcribe and summarise interviews. You still read the transcripts.
Cluster notes into themes and draft problem statements.
Generate dozens of "How might we" angles and moodboard images.
Turn a prompt or sketch into a first layout or working prototype.
Draft test scripts and summarise session notes.

hero.cap: A student exploring a virtual space with a VR headset and controllers.

media.alt: A standalone VR headset with two hand controllers on a desk
media.cap: A standalone VR headset and its two hand controllers.

p: A VR headset has two small screens, one for each eye, behind lenses that make the image fill your view. Sensors track your head so the world moves naturally when you look around.
The controllers track your hands. Many headsets can also follow your bare hands with cameras, so you can pinch and grab without controllers.
defs: Screens, lenses, speakers and tracking cameras in one unit.
Buttons, triggers and vibration (haptics) for your hands.
A safe, clear area you mark out so you don't walk into furniture.

media.alt: A phone shows a virtual armchair placed in a real living room
media.cap: AR on a phone: a virtual chair placed in a real room.

p: You don't need a headset for AR. Your phone camera shows the real world and the app adds digital objects on top. Furniture previews, face filters and Pokémon GO all work this way.

media.alt: A person in a mixed reality headset sees floating app windows in their living room
media.cap: Mixed reality: digital windows and objects placed in a real room.

p: A mixed reality headset shows your real room through cameras, then places digital windows and 3D objects in it. Those objects stay anchored, so a virtual screen stays on your wall even when you walk away.

Then loop back. Every test teaches you something new.
affinity: Write every observation on its own note
Spot notes that share a theme
Name each cluster. These become your insights.

scamper: Swap the login form for a student ID scan
Combine room booking with your class calendar
Adapt a restaurant waitlist for full study rooms
Show only the next free room, not a long list
Use booking data to show the quietest times
Drop the confirmation email and show a QR pass

fidelity: Low fidelity: a quick sketch. Is the idea understandable?
Mid fidelity: a grey-box wireframe. Is the layout right?
High fidelity: styled and clickable. Does it feel right?
users: Test with 1 user and you find about 31% of usability problems
5 users: about 85%. Fix what you found, then test again with five more.
proximity: Sixteen evenly spaced dots read as one block
Add space between rows and you see two groups of rows
Move the space between columns and you see two groups of columns
similarity: Same colour everywhere: just a grid
Colour alternate columns and you see columns
Colour alternate rows and the grid becomes rows
closure: Cut a wedge from each one…
…and your brain draws a triangle that isn't there
fitts: Large and close: fast and hard to miss
Small and far: slower, and easier to miss
hicks: 12 options: people hesitate. Group or hide what is rarely needed.
miller: Ten digits in a row are hard to hold in memory
Split into three chunks, the same digits are easy to remember
spectrum: Real world: an ordinary room with a desk
AR: digital information appears on top of the real room, usually through a phone
MR: a digital object sits on the real desk and stays anchored there
VR: the real room disappears and you are inside a fully digital world
comfort: Too close: hard to focus on and uncomfortable
Too far to the side: users have to turn their head
In front, at a comfortable distance: easy to read and reach
prompt: A vague prompt gets generic ideas back
Role: tell the AI who to be
Context: give it your real research
Task: say exactly what you need
Constraints: set limits on length and number
Format: say how to return it. Now the output is useful.
voice: Voice is fast for simple commands
A short confirmation tells the driver it worked
scamperWords: What could you borrow from elsewhere?
What could be bigger or smaller?
What if you flipped the order?
